name: Purified pollen cytoplasm extract (alone or with pumpkin seed and vitamin E)
short: Bee pollen, a different product: anaphylaxis in one case report. Pollen extract with pumpkin seed and vitamin E: adverse events few and mild. Purified extract: no allergy data or event counts.
text: Purified pollen cytoplasm extract, by mouth: a 2024 meta-analysis of 5 studies (1 randomised trial and 4 observational studies, 420 women) concluded that its use was not associated with significant adverse effects. In a 3-month placebo-controlled trial in 39 breast cancer survivors, side effects were recorded at each visit and the authors describe the extract as well tolerated; the abstract gives no numbers. In an open 3-month observational study in 104 menopausal women taking a pollen extract product with vitamin E, the authors report a very low side effect profile, also without numbers. A laboratory study in human liver microsomes found negligible inhibition of CYP2D6, the enzyme through which, the authors say, SSRI antidepressants can reduce the efficacy of tamoxifen; it did not test the extract in people taking tamoxifen. With pumpkin seed extract and vitamin E: in a 90-day placebo-controlled trial in 81 women with urinary incontinence, associated adverse events were few and mild in intensity. Allergy: none of these abstracts reports an allergic reaction or says whether people with pollen allergy were included. For bee pollen (pollen collected by bees, a different product), case reports describe a non-life-threatening anaphylactic reaction in an atopic woman on first swallowing a small amount, and an allergic reaction after eating it in a 4-year-old boy with seasonal rhinitis; those authors say foods derived from bees can be dangerous to people with pollen allergy. The abstracts do not say whether this applies to purified pollen extracts. No interaction data in people were found in the cited sources.
